prompt: Why do the bars of a histogram touch, while the bars of a chart of categories stand apart?
hint: What lies between two neighbouring bins?

choices.text: To save space on the page
choices.why: It is about meaning, not space: the gap or its absence says something about the variable.

choices.text: The bins are consecutive stretches of one number line
choices.why: Right. Nothing lies between two neighbouring bins, while nothing lies between two categories either, in a different sense: they have no order or distance.

choices.text: Histograms always have more bars
choices.why: A histogram can have five bars and a category chart twenty; the number is not the reason.

choices.text: Because the counts in a histogram are larger
choices.why: The heights have nothing to do with whether the bars touch.

prompt: A peak appears in a histogram with bins of 5 minutes and vanishes with bins of 4 and of 6. What is the best reading?
hint: Does the shape survive a small change?

choices.text: Bins of 5 minutes are the correct width
choices.why: There is no single correct width; a feature that depends on one width is suspect.

choices.text: The data has two groups
choices.why: A real second group would show at neighbouring widths too.

choices.text: Probably chance, not a feature of the data
choices.why: Right. A shape that does not survive small changes in the bin width was probably never there.

choices.text: The data was recorded wrongly at those times
choices.why: Nothing suggests an error; the bins are what changed, not the data.

prompt: Values run from 0 to 440. How many bins of width 20 cover that range?
A distribution has its peak on the left and a long tail stretching right. What is it called?
hint: Which part gives the shape its name?

choices.text: Left-skewed, because the peak is on the left
choices.why: The name follows the tail, not the peak.

choices.text: Right-skewed
choices.why: Right. The direction of a skew is the direction of its tail.

choices.text: Symmetric, as it has one peak
choices.why: One peak says nothing about symmetry; the two sides fall away differently.

choices.text: Bimodal
choices.why: Bimodal means two peaks.

prompt: For which of these quantities would you expect a left-skewed distribution?
hint: Look for a quantity with a ceiling most values approach.

choices.text: The money customers spend per order
choices.why: Money has a floor and no ceiling, which gives a tail to the right.

choices.text: The time customers wait on the phone
choices.why: Waiting times are bounded below by zero and stretch up, so they skew right.

choices.text: Scores on a test most people find easy
choices.why: Right. Scores pile up against the maximum, and a few low ones form a tail to the left.

choices.text: The weights of bags from a well-adjusted filling machine
choices.why: Small random misses either side of the target give a symmetric shape.

prompt: A data set's mean is 52 and its median 61. If it has a single peak, which shape is most likely?
hint: Which way does a tail pull the mean?

choices.text: Left-skewed
choices.why: Right. A tail of low values pulls the mean below the median.

choices.text: Right-skewed, with the mean dragged up by a tail
choices.why: A right tail would put the mean above the median, not below.

choices.text: Symmetric, since a 9-point gap is small
choices.why: Nine points on a median of 61 is a wide gap for a one-peaked shape.

choices.text: It cannot be told without a histogram
choices.why: For one-peaked data the order of mean and median is a fair guide.

prompt: Why does the skewness formula cube the deviations instead of squaring them?
hint: What happens to the sign of −3 when squared, and when cubed?

choices.text: To make the result larger and easier to read
choices.why: The size is standardised away; the cube is about the sign.

choices.text: Because squares are already used up by the variance
choices.why: Nothing is used up; squares would simply lose the direction of the deviations.

choices.text: To give values near the mean more weight
choices.why: Cubing gives far values more weight, not near ones.

choices.text: Cubes keep the sign, so the two sides pull against each other
choices.why: Right. Far values above and below push the total in opposite directions, and whichever side is longer wins.

prompt: A data set has mean 40, median 34 and standard deviation 12. What is Pearson's median skewness, 3 × (mean − median) ÷ sd?
The skewness of Horta's 400 baskets is 2.10. How would the rough guide describe it?
hint: Sign for direction, size for strength.

choices.text: Roughly symmetric
choices.why: That band is between −0.5 and 0.5.

choices.text: Moderately left-skewed
choices.why: A positive skewness means a tail to the right.

choices.text: Strongly right-skewed
choices.why: Right. Positive and beyond 1: a long tail of large baskets.

choices.text: Moderately right-skewed, between 0.5 and 1
choices.why: 2.10 is well beyond 1.

prompt: Two distributions have the same mean and standard deviation. One has an excess kurtosis of 6, the other of 0. What differs?
hint: Kurtosis is mostly about one part of the distribution.

choices.text: The first is more spread out
choices.why: Their standard deviations are equal; kurtosis is about where the spread comes from.

choices.text: Extreme values are more common in the first
choices.why: Right. Heavy tails: more of its spread comes from rare values far from the mean.

choices.text: The first is skewed to the right
choices.why: Skewness is a separate number; both could be symmetric.

choices.text: The first has a flat top
choices.why: High kurtosis is about tails, and the heavy-tailed curve here is taller in the middle, not flatter.

prompt: In the fourth-power calculation, how many times as much does a value 3 standard deviations from the mean contribute as one at 1 standard deviation?
Kurtosis minus 3, which scores 0 for the normal shape, is called ___ kurtosis.
hint: What is left over beyond the normal's.

prompt: A risk model assumes losses follow the normal shape. The real losses have an excess kurtosis of 5. What will the model get wrong?
hint: Heavy tails are where surprises live.

choices.text: It will overstate the typical loss
choices.why: Kurtosis is about the tails, not the typical value.

choices.text: Nothing, since mean and standard deviation are what matter
choices.why: Equal mean and standard deviation can hide very different tails.

choices.text: It will predict losses that are too large
choices.why: The opposite: it will treat large losses as rarer than they are.

choices.text: It will call large losses far rarer than they really are
choices.why: Right. Heavy tails make extreme values much more common than the normal shape allows.

prompt: Order times peak at 12:00 and at 19:30, with almost nothing in the afternoon. The mean order time is 16:06. What is wrong with reporting it?

choices.text: The arithmetic is wrong
choices.why: The arithmetic is fine; the trouble is what it describes.

choices.text: It falls where almost nobody orders
choices.why: Right. A mean of two groups describes neither, and here it lands in the empty afternoon.

choices.text: Times of day cannot be averaged
choices.why: They can be; the mean of these ones just describes nothing useful.

choices.text: The median should be used, because it is robust
choices.why: The median, 17:57, also misses both peaks. Two groups need two summaries.

prompt: What is the most useful first step with clearly bimodal data?
hint: Two peaks usually mean two of something.

choices.text: Report the mean and the standard deviation as usual
choices.why: Both describe the mixture, which is a distribution nobody experiences.

choices.text: Remove the smaller peak as outliers
choices.why: A whole peak of real values is a group, not a set of errors.

choices.text: Use wider bins until there is one peak
choices.why: That hides the most interesting thing in the data.

choices.text: Find what separates the two groups
choices.why: Right. Two peaks usually mean two groups; finding the variable that splits them is worth more than any summary.

prompt: A boxplot of order times looks completely ordinary, and the excess kurtosis is −1.69. What should you do?
hint: What can the histogram show that the boxplot cannot?

choices.text: Nothing: an ordinary boxplot means an ordinary distribution
choices.why: A boxplot cannot show two peaks, so an ordinary-looking one proves nothing.

choices.text: Draw the histogram
choices.why: Right. Strongly negative kurtosis hints at humps away from the centre, and only the histogram shows them.

choices.text: Report the median, which is robust to the tails
choices.why: Robustness to tails does not help when the problem is two peaks.

choices.text: Conclude the data has heavy tails
choices.why: Negative excess kurtosis means light tails, not heavy ones.
